title: Algorithm Design
summary: How to design an efficient algorithm for a new problem, prove it correct and bound its running time, using four paradigms: greedy, divide and conquer, dynamic programming and network flow. The course follows Kleinberg and Tardos, chapters 4 to 7, with lectures, skill-circuit exercises on WebLab and tutorials. You are graded on two written exams (proofs, traces, recurrences) and one three-hour programming exam in Java on WebLab.

basis.description: Slides of all 16 CSE2310 lectures of 2024-25 as text, the CSE2310 assignments and peer-review exercises, and the past papers. Time shares count content slides of Lectures 1 to 14; course organisation, asides and the two written-exam preparation lectures (15 and 16) are left out.
basis.caveat: The material is from CSE2310, taught in quarter 2; from 2026-27 the course is CSE21B in year 2, quarter 1, with the same content. Slide counts understate network flow: it had 4 of the 14 content lectures (about 29 percent of the lecture slots) but much of it was worked on the blackboard, while the divide and conquer and dynamic programming slides build up examples frame by frame.

topics.name: Asymptotics, graphs and proof foundations
know: Big-O, Big-Omega and Big-Theta, how polynomials, logarithms and exponentials compare, and what a tight bound means
Graph representations, BFS and DFS, connected components and bipartiteness testing, all in O(n + m)
DAGs and topological ordering: every DAG has a node without incoming edges, and a graph is a DAG exactly when it has a topological order
Proof by induction, by contradiction and by counterexample, as used in every later correctness proof
do: Give a tight bound for nested loops and for loops that halve or double a counter
Compute a topological order and prove the lemmas behind the algorithm
pitfalls: Giving a loose upper bound when a tight one is asked: the written papers ask for tight bounds and deduct for slower algorithms

topics.name: Greedy scheduling, caching and Huffman codes
know: Interval scheduling (earliest finish time first) and interval partitioning (by start time, as many resources as the depth)
Minimising maximum lateness: earliest deadline first, schedules without idle time, and inversions
Optimal offline caching with farthest-in-future eviction, and why least-recently-used can be worse
Huffman codes: prefix codes as full binary trees, merging the two lowest frequencies, and why the lowest two are siblings at the deepest level
The two proof patterns: greedy stays ahead (induction on a measure) and the exchange argument (swap adjacent inversions without making the solution worse)
How to measure a running time experimentally and compare it with the analysis
do: Disprove a proposed sorting rule with a small counterexample, then find the rule that works
Write a complete exchange-argument or stays-ahead proof with notation for the greedy and an optimal solution
Trace farthest-in-future eviction or build a Huffman tree and code table by hand
Implement a greedy algorithm in O(n log n) with sorting or a priority queue
pitfalls: Defining an inversion without the inequality between the two jobs, a mistake the marking notes list often
Ending an exchange proof without a valid contradiction, or with an assumption whose negation does not say that greedy is optimal
Swapping in the greedy order instead of turning an optimal solution into the greedy one: the marking notes cap that at partial credit

topics.name: Minimum spanning trees, shortest paths and clustering
know: Dijkstra's algorithm for non-negative edge weights and its O(m log n) running time with a heap
The cut property (the cheapest edge across any cut is in every MST, with distinct weights) and the cycle property (the most expensive edge on a cycle is in no MST)
Prim (Prim-Jarnik) and Kruskal, and why each is correct by one of the two properties
Union-find with union by size or rank, and Kruskal in O(m log n)
k-clustering of maximum spacing: run Kruskal and stop at k components, or delete the k - 1 most expensive MST edges
do: Apply the cut or cycle property to a cut or cycle you choose and state what it says about the MST
Run Prim, Kruskal or Dijkstra by hand and give the order in which edges or nodes are added
Find the optimal k-clustering of a small graph and its spacing
Implement Kruskal with a union-find structure for a clustering or MST question
pitfalls: Using the cycle property on an edge that is not the heaviest of its cycle, or stating the cut property for an edge that does not cross the cut

topics.name: Divide and conquer and recurrences
lectures: Lecture 7 - Divide and Conquer Part 3 (Exam Prep)
know: The three steps divide, solve and combine, and how the cost of the combine step sets the running time
Mergesort, counting inversions and fast exponentiation by repeated squaring
The master theorem for T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n): compare f(n) with n to the power log_b a, the three cases, and the regularity condition
Unrolling a recurrence as a recursion tree when the master theorem does not apply
Course examples: prefix sums, the longest common prefix of n strings, maximum subarray, quickselect for the k-th largest element
Book topics that also appear on papers: closest pair of points and Karatsuba integer multiplication
do: Solve a recurrence with the master theorem, naming a, b, f(n), the case and the result, for example T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n^3 gives Theta(n^3 log n)
Design a divide and conquer algorithm for a new problem and state its recurrence
Count the multiplications fast exponentiation needs for a given exponent
Implement a recursive solution that returns extra information from each half, such as the minimum, the maximum and the best answer
pitfalls: Skipping the step that compares f(n) with n to the power log_b a: each step of the master method earns its own point
Returning only the answer from each recursive call when the combine step needs more information, so the merge becomes too slow

topics.name: Dynamic programming
know: Overlapping subproblems as the difference with divide and conquer; memoisation versus iterative (bottom-up) filling
Weighted interval scheduling with the predecessor p(j): OPT(j) = max(OPT(j - 1), v_j + OPT(p(j)))
0/1 knapsack and subset sum with a second parameter for remaining capacity, in O(nW) pseudo-polynomial time
Sequence alignment with gap and mismatch costs, and the RNA secondary structure recurrence over intervals
Course examples: maximum subarray, the bitcoin and euro trading days, longest path in a DAG, word segmentation
Recovering the solution from a filled table by walking back through the choices
Space saving: keep only the rows or entries the recurrence looks back at; Bellman-Ford for shortest paths with negative edges
do: Write a recursive OPT function with base cases, recursive cases and the initial call for a new problem
Add a parameter to a known recurrence for an extra constraint (at most k items of a type, at least K days of work)
Fill a memoisation table by hand and trace back which items or intervals were chosen
State the time and the minimal space of the iterative version, and the loop order that fills it
Implement an iterative solution in Java, and reconstruct a solution from a given table
pitfalls: Base cases that do not match the initial call, or that return plus infinity where a maximum is taken
Forgetting how to call the function after adding a parameter, which costs its own point
Filling a two-index interval table in the wrong order: the outer loop must grow the interval length

topics.name: Flow networks, cuts and Ford-Fulkerson
know: Flow networks, capacity and conservation constraints, s-t cuts and their capacity
The flow value lemma, weak duality (any flow is at most any cut) and the max-flow min-cut theorem
Residual graphs with forward and backward edges, augmenting paths, and the integrality theorem
Ford-Fulkerson in O(mC), capacity scaling in O(m^2 log C), and Edmonds-Karp with BFS in O(nm^2)
Finding a minimum cut from a maximum flow: the nodes reachable from s in the residual graph
do: Run Ford-Fulkerson or the scaling version by hand and show the flow after each phase
Read a minimum cut and its capacity off a given maximum flow
Change one capacity so a given flow is no longer maximum, and show the augmenting path
Give a tight running time for building a network and running Ford-Fulkerson on it
pitfalls: In the scaling version, using edges whose residual capacity is below the current delta

topics.name: Network flow modelling and circulations
know: Bipartite matching and assignment models: source to one side, capacities as limits, and reading the assignment off edges with flow 1
Circulations with supplies and demands, and lower bounds on edges
Removing lower bounds: subtract the lower bound from the capacity and adjust the demands at both ends, then add a super source and sink
Min-cut models for two-way splits: image segmentation and project selection, where the cut capacity equals the cost to minimise
Course and book applications: baseball elimination, the train allocation and judo camp problems, edge-disjoint paths, survey design
The provided Java library: maximizeFlow and hasCirculation on Graph, Node and Edge classes
do: Model a word problem as a network: nodes, edges, capacities and lower bounds, and how the answer follows from the flow
Prove that a model is correct in both directions, or that the minimum cut equals the optimum
Turn a circulation with lower bounds into an ordinary max-flow instance, showing the steps
Implement a model with the library in WebLab and return a yes or no answer or an assignment
pitfalls: Adding only an infinite edge from t to s when lower bounds appear, and losing the requirement that every item is assigned
Giving a zero circulation as a counterexample when two different non-zero circulations are needed
Dropping one of several bounds in a model: the reference code tests versions that ignore one bound

prerequisites: Algorithms and Data Structures: graphs, BFS and DFS, sorting, heaps and asymptotic analysis
Reasoning and Logic: proof by induction and by contradiction
Java programming fluent enough to write an algorithm from scratch under time pressure
Basic logarithm and sum rules, such as 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^(k-1) = 2^k - 1
practical: There are no graded labs. Each module has a skill circuit on WebLab with implementation exercises at exam level that are checked automatically, written assignments with peer and TA review, and Acing AD sessions with old exam problems. A network flow library (Graph, Node, Edge, maximizeFlow, hasCirculation) is built in the tutorials and handed out in the programming exam.
studyAdvice: Split your time evenly between written and programming practice: each half counts for 50 percent, and a half below 5 caps your grade at that mark.
Revise greedy and divide and conquer before the first written exam (week 5); the second covers only dynamic programming and network flow.
Give network flow more time than its slides suggest: it had four lectures, and a modelling task appears on every analysed paper, with lower bounds on five of the six.
Learn the two greedy proof templates by heart and practise writing them out with full notation; each costs 5 points on a resit.
For dynamic programming, practise the full chain: define the subproblem, write OPT with base cases and the initial call, fill a table by hand, then code it iteratively.
Do the skill-circuit programming exercises in WebLab under a time limit; the exam gives no book or notes, only the Java API.
Work through old written papers first without the book, then check with it, as the course page advises.
